questions.title: Does § 1216(a)(3)’s “shall … conduct an investigation” language create a judicially enforceable procedural right for complainants?
questions.question_body: The opinion suggests AFL framed its claim as deprivation of a procedural right to an OSC investigation under 5 U.S.C. § 1216(a)(3), but the court says a bare procedural right in vacuo doesn’t confer standing (citing Summers). I’m confused: when a statute says OSC “shall … conduct an investigation” of arbitrary FOIA withholdings, why isn’t that enough to be a concrete procedural entitlement for the complainant? Is the problem that § 1216 directs OSC’s duties without creating any corresponding right in requesters, or that even mandatory procedures still require a separate concrete interest tied to the procedure?

questions.title: Why doesn’t informational standing attach to the notices and updates AFL hoped to receive if OSC investigated under § 1216?
questions.question_body: The court says informational standing requires a statute that entitles the plaintiff to receive information, and concludes § 1216 creates no such entitlement. AFL argued that if OSC investigated under § 1216, it might choose to provide the notifications that § 1214 requires in prohibited personnel practice cases. Given § 1216(c) says OSC may investigate and seek corrective action “under § 1214 … in the same way,” why doesn’t that incorporate § 1214’s notice requirements? Is Carson v. OSC controlling nationwide that § 1214’s procedures are discretionary in § 1216 investigations, and if so, what statutory text makes those notices optional rather than mandatory?

questions.title: How exactly do causation and redressability fail when the requested relief is just an order that OSC investigate?
questions.question_body: The opinion describes a speculative causal chain: if OSC investigated, it might pursue corrective/disciplinary action; the MSPB might sanction; DOJ might change course; and thus AFL might get records. In procedural-injury cases courts relax imminence and redressability somewhat. Why didn’t that relaxed standard suffice here? Are there examples where a court found standing to compel a preliminary procedural step even though ultimate relief depended on independent actors? What distinguishes those cases from this one?

questions.title: How are § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) (FOIA’s OSC referral provision) and § 1216 (general OSC authority) supposed to interact?
questions.question_body: The district court held that FOIA’s three triggers in § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) do not limit OSC’s authority under § 1216 to investigate arbitrary or capricious FOIA withholdings. The D.C. Circuit didn’t reach merits but recites that holding. Statutorily, is § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) best read as an additional mandatory-investigation pathway when its predicates are met, without precluding § 1216 investigations otherwise? If so, what is the practical difference between a § 1216-initiated investigation and a § 552(a)(4)(F)(i)-triggered one, especially regarding what information, if any, must be shared with the complainant?

questions.title: Could the district court properly remand to OSC for reconsideration if Article III standing was lacking from the start?
questions.question_body: The district court said OSC committed a legal error in reading § 552(a)(4)(F)(i) to limit § 1216, but then declined to order an investigation and instead remanded to OSC. The D.C. Circuit vacated for lack of standing. Under Steel Co., courts must assure jurisdiction before reaching the merits. Was the district court’s remand itself a merits-based action taken without jurisdiction? More generally, can a court remand to an agency for further consideration if the plaintiff lacks standing, or must it dismiss outright without any substantive guidance?

questions.title: Is there any scenario where a FOIA requester would have standing to compel OSC action under § 1216?
questions.question_body: The panel emphasizes problems of traceability and redressability and the lack of a statutory entitlement to information from OSC. Hypothetically, could a requester ever show standing to force a § 1216 investigation—for example, if OSC’s own regulations promised complainant updates, or if the requester could allege facts making MSPB or agency action sufficiently likely? Or is Chaney’s enforcement-discretion presumption and the lack of a complainant-facing entitlement under § 1216 a categorical bar?

questions.title: What counts as the requisite “concrete, particularized interest” tied to the alleged procedural violation in this setting?
questions.question_body: The court says even under the relaxed procedural-injury framework, AFL must show the violation of a procedural right affected a concrete, particularized interest. If the interest is access to DOJ records, the court says that’s traceable to DOJ, not OSC. If the interest is the investigation’s information, the court says there’s no entitlement. What kind of concrete interest could satisfy this requirement in an OSC-investigation context—e.g., would a federal employee whistleblower alleging a prohibited personnel practice have a different result because § 1214 gives them specific notification rights?

questions.title: Does Heckler v. Chaney effectively swallow § 1216’s mandatory ‘shall investigate’ language for reviewability purposes?
questions.question_body: The opinion leans on Chaney to highlight the judiciary’s inability to compel agency enforcement choices and uses that to show redressability is speculative. But § 1216(a)(3) says OSC “shall … conduct an investigation” of allegations about arbitrary FOIA withholdings. When, if ever, is a ‘shall investigate’ command judicially enforceable post-Chaney? Is the idea that the initial decision to open an investigation might be reviewable if truly mandatory, but choices about seeking corrective/disciplinary action are not—or does Chaney’s presumption extend even to the threshold investigation decision when the statute lacks complainant-facing rights and standards?
